729.title: The kingdom splits (1 Kings 12)
729.hook: a young king ignores the old counselors and the kingdom tears in two
729.howItsDone: Some Christians read Rehoboam's story as a warning about pride and about choosing advisers who only say what we want, and the old men's counsel to be a servant is sometimes linked to Jesus's teaching on servant leadership.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Solomon, admitting his house could never hold God. Your line was heaven cannot contain you.

"Thy father made our yoke grievous." Solomon is dead, and his son Rehoboam has gone to Shechem to be made king. The people bring one request, in the King James words: make the heavy yoke your father put on us lighter, "and we will serve thee." That's the deal on the table. Lighten the load, and you have a kingdom. Rehoboam doesn't answer on the spot. He tells them to come back in three days. And in those three days he asks for advice twice, from two very different tables.

First he goes to the old men who stood before his father Solomon while he lived. Their answer is a paradox: "If thou wilt be a servant unto this people this day, and wilt serve them, and answer them, and speak good words to them, then they will be thy servants for ever." Serve them today, and they'll serve you for good. Then he goes to the young men who grew up with him. Their answer is the opposite: talk tough. "My little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins." And: "my father hath chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions." The text puts the choice in one line: he "forsook the counsel of the old men." He asked the old ones first, heard the answer, set it aside, and asked again. On the third day he gives the people the young men's speech, word for word. And the people answer with a cry that tears the kingdom: "What portion have we in David? ... to your tents, O Israel: now see to thine own house, David." The northern tribes walk away and make Jeroboam their king; only Judah stays with the house of David. The text holds two things together. Rehoboam made a choice. And "the cause was from the LORD," fulfilling a word a prophet had already spoken. Readers weigh those two lines differently, but nobody in the story pretends the choice wasn't his. The old men's advice cost nothing but pride: one soft answer, one lighter yoke. He couldn't pay it.
screen: `HE FORSOOK THE COUNSEL OF THE OLD MEN.`

segments.voice: Hold one decision that's in front of you, and then bring to mind someone older who has seen more of life than you: a parent, a grandparent, a neighbor, a retired coworker. Hear, as honestly as you can, what they'd probably say, and ask yourself: is that the answer I'm avoiding? If you pray, bring both the decision and the person before God.
Rehoboam. The young king who heard the old men say be a servant, chose the young men's threat instead, and watched the people go to their tents.
Your line: listen to the old ones. Two tables, and he went with the second. See you tomorrow.

730.title: Fed by ravens (1 Kings 17:1–7)
730.hook: Elijah hides by a brook, and ravens bring bread and meat
730.howItsDone: Some Christians read Elijah and the ravens as a picture of God's daily provision, and the story is sometimes paired with Jesus's words about the ravens in Luke 12 when churches teach about worry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rehoboam, a young king who set aside the old men's counsel. Your line was listen to the old ones.

Bread and meat, twice a day, delivered by birds. But first a man walks into the story out of nowhere. No birth story, no call. Just a name, Elijah the Tishbite, of Gilead, and a sentence to Ahab, the king of Israel: "As the LORD God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word." Then, just as suddenly, the word comes to Elijah: get out of here. Turn east. Hide yourself by the brook Cherith, near the Jordan.

Here's the promise, in the King James Bible: "thou shalt drink of the brook; and I have commanded the ravens to feed thee there." He goes, and it happens: "the ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening; and he drank of the brook." Three things are worth slowing down for. First, the delivery service. In the law of Moses, the raven is on the list of birds Israel was not to eat: "Every raven after his kind." So the prophet's bread comes in the beak of a bird his own law kept off the table. Help from an unexpected quarter. Second, Elijah has to receive it. A man who has just faced down a king sits by a stream and waits for birds. There's no way to earn this meal, only to be there when it comes. Third, it doesn't last. "And it came to pass after a while, that the brook dried up, because there had been no rain in the land." The drought Elijah announced reaches him too. The ravens were for a season, not forever, and tomorrow's story begins because the water ran out. Much later, Jesus points at the same birds when he talks about worry. In Luke's Gospel he says: "Consider the ravens: for they neither sow nor reap; which neither have storehouse nor barn; and God feedeth them." Some readers hear the two passages together: the bird that is fed, and the bird that feeds a prophet.
screen: `AFTER A WHILE, THE BROOK DRIED UP.`

segments.voice: Think back to help you got from a source you'd never have chosen: a stranger, someone you didn't much like, a setback that turned out to carry something. Then ask whether help is being offered now that you've been too proud, or too wary, to take, and just picture receiving it. If you pray, give thanks for one raven in your life.

731.title: The widow's jar (1 Kings 17:8–16)
731.hook: a starving widow shares her last cake, and the flour doesn't run out
731.howItsDone: Some Christians tell the story of the widow of Zarephath when they talk about generosity in hard times, and Jesus's mention of her in Luke 4 is sometimes read alongside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, at Cherith, ravens fed Elijah until the brook dried up. Your line was the ravens came.

A woman is picking up sticks at the gate of a town called Zarephath. Two sticks, the text says. Enough for one small fire. The brook has dried up, and the word has come to Elijah: go to Zarephath, "behold, I have commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee." The ravens were commanded. Now it's a widow, and she doesn't seem to know it. Zarephath isn't in Israel. It belongs to Zidon, the country Queen Jezebel comes from. Elijah, a stranger and a foreigner, asks her for a little water, and then, as she turns to get it, a piece of bread.

Her answer, in the King James Bible, is stark: "As the LORD thy God liveth, I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse: and, behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die." One small word: thy God. Not mine. Yours. She is not of Elijah's people, and she expects this to be the last meal she and her son will eat. Elijah says something that sounds outrageous: "Fear not; go and do as thou hast said: but make me thereof a little cake first." Then the promise: "The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the day that the LORD sendeth rain upon the earth." And the text says it plainly: she went and did according to the saying of Elijah. She gives from her last, to a foreigner, on the strength of a promise from a God she calls his. And "the barrel of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail." The text never says the barrel overflowed. The meal simply doesn't run out: "she, and he, and her house, did eat many days." Enough, not more. In Luke's Gospel, Jesus remembers her: there were many widows in Israel in that famine, but Elijah was sent to none of them except this one, a widow in Sarepta, a city of Sidon.

Name something you don't have much of right now, time, money, patience, energy, and notice how tightly you're holding it. Then picture one person who could use a small piece of it, not all of it, a handful: a phone call, a meal, an hour, a kind word. If you pray, you can bring that person before God.
Zarephath. The town where a widow fed a stranger from her last handful, and the meal and oil were there each day, until the rain.
Your line: the jar did not fail. A handful of meal, shared first, and it lasted. Day seven hundred thirty-one, done.

732.title: Fire on Carmel (1 Kings 18:20–39)
732.hook: how long will you limp between two opinions? water-soaked wood, and fire falls
732.howItsDone: Some Christians read Elijah on Mount Carmel in sermons on wholehearted faith, and his question about halting between two opinions is sometimes quoted when preachers speak about indecision.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zarephath: meal and oil that did not run out, until the rain. Your line was the jar did not fail.

"How long halt ye between two opinions?" Halt is an older English word for limp. How long will you limp along, one foot on each side? Elijah says it on Mount Carmel, to a crowd of his own people, gathered by the king. On one side stand the prophets of Baal, the god the king and queen have favored. On the other, Elijah, alone. "If the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him." And the line that hangs in the air: "the people answered him not a word."

Elijah proposes a test. Two altars, two bulls, wood, and no fire. "The God that answereth by fire, let him be God." The people finally speak: "It is well spoken." The prophets of Baal go first, calling from morning until noon, and on into the afternoon. The report is short: "there was no voice, nor any that answered." Then Elijah repairs the altar of the LORD that had been broken down, with twelve stones, one for each tribe of the sons of Jacob, in a kingdom now split in two. Then he has water poured over the offering and the wood, and again, and a third time, until it fills the trench. His prayer is short: "Hear me, O LORD, hear me, that this people may know that thou art the LORD God, and that thou hast turned their heart back again." In the line before, he asks that Israel know he is God's servant, yes, but the prayer ends on the people: their hearts, turned back. And the fire falls. It "consumed the burnt sacrifice, and the wood, and the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench." The people fall on their faces: "The LORD, he is the God; the LORD, he is the God." The silence has become an answer. The chapter goes on to a grim ending at the brook Kishon, and readers have wrestled with it. But at its center is the question Elijah asked first, about limping: a life with one foot on each side, never quite choosing.

Bring to mind one decision you've been circling for a while, a conversation to have or not, a commitment to keep or end, and notice the limp: one foot on each side. You don't have to settle it now; just name the very next step that would end the waiting. If you pray, you can bring the decision before God.
Carmel. The mountain where Elijah asked a silent crowd how long they'd limp between two opinions, soaked his altar, prayed, and watched the fire fall.
Your line: how long, two opinions? A silent crowd, and then a cry. Until tomorrow.

733.title: Under the broom tree (1 Kings 19:1–8)
733.hook: exhausted, Elijah wants to die; an angel says eat and sleep
733.carry: the journey is too great for you
733.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Elijah under the broom tree in times of burnout or depression, and pastors sometimes point to the angel's care, food and sleep before any words, as a model for caring for the exhausted.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Carmel, and a crowd limping between two opinions until the fire fell. Your line was how long, two opinions?

One chapter after fire falls from heaven, Elijah is running for his life. Ahab tells Queen Jezebel everything that happened on Carmel, and she sends Elijah a message: by this time tomorrow, you'll be as dead as the prophets you killed. And the man who stood alone against a crowd simply runs. The text says "he arose, and went for his life." To Beer-sheba, in Judah. He leaves his servant there, walks one more day, alone, into the wilderness, and sits down under a desert bush.

Under the bush, Elijah asks to die. In the King James Bible: "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers." The King James calls the bush a juniper tree; other translations say broom tree. The Bible doesn't hide this moment. A prophet who has just seen fire from heaven is so spent he wants it all to stop. Some readers find that honesty a comfort in itself. He lies down and sleeps. An angel touches him and says only: "Arise and eat." By his head there's "a cake baken on the coals, and a cruse of water." He eats, he drinks, and he lies down again. The angel lets him. Then a second touch, and the line we carry today: "Arise and eat; because the journey is too great for thee." No argument. No lecture about Carmel. No correction of his prayer. First sleep, then bread and water, then sleep again, then more bread. When the angel finally speaks about the road ahead, it's to agree with him: yes, this is too much for you. Not as a rebuke. As a reason to eat. He "went in the strength of that meat forty days and forty nights unto Horeb the mount of God." The big conversation waits until he has been fed. One more thing, said plainly: if tiredness ever turns into wanting your life to end, that's the moment to tell someone today, a friend, a doctor, or a crisis line where you live.
screen: `IT IS ENOUGH; TAKE AWAY MY LIFE.`
`THE JOURNEY IS TOO GREAT FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself three plain questions, the angel's kind: When did I last eat something real? When did I last drink water? How did I sleep? Don't judge the answers, and set one pressing decision gently to one side until after a meal and a night's sleep; if you pray, rest in the words arise and eat.
broom tree. The desert bush where spent and afraid, Elijah asked to die, and an angel answered with bread, water, sleep, and a second touch.
Your line: the journey is too great for you. The angel brought bread before any advice. Rest well.

734.title: Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21)
734.hook: a king and queen seize a man's family land by lies
734.howItsDone: Some Christians point to Naboth's vineyard when they speak up about land seizure, eviction and abuse of power, and churches sometimes read it alongside the prophets' warnings about those who add field to field.

segments.voice: Yesterday, under the broom tree: bread, water, sleep, and a second touch. Your line was the journey is too great for you.
screen: `THE JOURNEY IS TOO GREAT FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: "The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee." That's a man named Naboth, saying no to a king. His vineyard sits right next to King Ahab's palace in Jezreel, and Ahab wants it for a vegetable garden. He even makes a fair offer: a better vineyard, or the full price in money. Naboth refuses. And the king of Israel goes home, lies down on his bed, turns his face away, and won't eat. Over a garden.

To Naboth it isn't real estate. It's inheritance, the land his family has held, and the law of Moses treats land that way. In Leviticus, God says: "The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine." Some things are not for sale, even to a king. Now Queen Jezebel finds her husband sulking, and says, "Dost thou now govern the kingdom of Israel?" I'll get you the vineyard. What she does is chilling because it all looks legal. She writes letters in Ahab's name and seals them with his seal. She has the elders of the city proclaim a fast, set Naboth on high among the people, and set two men across from him to accuse him. They say he blasphemed God and the king. The crowd takes him outside the city and stones him to death. Letters, seals, a public fast, witnesses: every piece of a proper trial, used for theft and murder. Then Ahab goes down to take possession of his garden, and there Elijah meets him, with a question that strips the paperwork away: "Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?" Ahab's reply is almost a confession: "Hast thou found me, O mine enemy?" And Elijah says, "I have found thee." The chapter doesn't end in simple triumph. When Ahab hears the judgment, he tears his clothes, fasts, and goes about quietly, and the text says God takes notice that he has humbled himself. But the vineyard stays a name for something people still see: the powerful taking a home through lies dressed as law.
screen: `THE LAND SHALL NOT BE SOLD FOR EVER.`

segments.voice: Picture someone losing their place: a neighbor facing eviction, a family pushed out by rising rent, people driven from their land by war, an aging parent leaving the house they raised you in. Stay with them at their front door without looking away, then ask what one real thing you could do. If you pray, you can hold them before God.
Naboth's vineyard. A man won't sell his family's land, and a king and queen take it with forged letters and false witnesses, until a prophet names it.
Your line: not for sale. A small vineyard, and a prophet who would not look away. That's day seven hundred thirty-four.

735.title: The chariot of fire (2 Kings 2:1–14)
735.hook: Elisha won't leave Elijah and asks for a double portion of his spirit
735.howItsDone: Some Christians speak of 'passing the mantle' when one generation of leaders hands on to the next, and some churches echo Elisha's request for a double portion when they pray for new leaders.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Naboth's vineyard, and a prophet who told a king, I have found thee. Your line was not for sale.

Two men are on the road out of Gilgal, an old prophet and his student. Elijah stops and says, "Tarry here, I pray thee." Stay here; the LORD has sent me on to Bethel. At Bethel, a company of prophets asks Elisha: don't you know the LORD will take your master from you today? His answer is short: "Yea, I know it; hold ye your peace." And Elijah says it again: tarry here. And again.

Three times Elijah tells him to stay behind: at Gilgal, at Bethel, at Jericho. Three times Elisha gives the same answer, in the King James words: "As the LORD liveth, and as thy soul liveth, I will not leave thee." They walk on to the Jordan. Elijah takes his mantle, his cloak, rolls it up, and strikes the water, and it parts, and they cross on dry ground. Across the river, Elijah turns to him: "Ask what I shall do for thee, before I be taken away from thee." Elisha doesn't ask small: "I pray thee, let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me." Some readers hear an echo of the law in Deuteronomy, where the firstborn son receives a double portion: Elisha is asking to be his heir. Elijah is honest: "Thou hast asked a hard thing." But if you see me when I'm taken, it will be yours. As they walk, a chariot of fire and horses of fire come between them, "and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven." The text is exact here: the chariot parted them, and the whirlwind took him up. Elisha cries out, "My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof." He tears his own clothes in two. Then he picks up the mantle that fell from Elijah, walks back to the Jordan, and strikes the water with it, asking, "Where is the LORD God of Elijah?" The water parts. The one who wouldn't leave is the one left holding the mantle. He stayed to the end, he asked plainly, and he saw.
screen: `I WILL NOT LEAVE THEE, THREE TIMES.`
`WHERE IS THE LORD GOD OF ELIJAH?`

segments.voice: Think of someone who taught you how to live, or work, or believe: a parent, a coach, a pastor. If they're still here, ask yourself what you'd want to ask of them, plainly, before it's too late; if they're gone, ask what mantle they left in your hands. If you pray, give thanks for them by name.
Mantle. Elijah's cloak, which parted the Jordan and then fell to Elisha, who refused to leave his teacher and asked for a double portion of his spirit.
Your line: I will not leave you. A week from a kingdom torn in two, through ravens, a widow's jar, Carmel, a broom tree and a stolen vineyard, to a chariot of fire. A full week.
